vignette:
At 57, he still thinks of his life as divided into before and after the accident. Before, he is a man who moves easily through other people’s homes and imagines how they might feel more open, more beautiful, more livable. As an interior designer, he spends decades noticing proportion, texture, color, and light. He is known for being calm under pressure, the one who can walk into a cramped, half-finished room and see possibility. He is divorced, lives alone, and takes a certain pride in the order of his apartment—chairs angled just so, books stacked cleanly, fabric samples arranged by tone. He says he has always believed that if a space is thoughtfully arranged, a person can breathe better in it.

The accident happens on an ordinary weekday, the kind of day he does not expect to remember. He is driving back from a client meeting with rolls of plans in the passenger seat, thinking about flooring samples and whether a dining room needs warmer lighting. Traffic slows abruptly on the highway. He brakes, feels the car skid, then hears the violent crack of impact from behind before he fully understands what is happening. His car lurches forward, metal folding around him. For a moment there is only noise—glass breaking, tires shrieking, a horn that will not stop. He smells something sharp and chemical. He cannot catch his breath. He is pinned at an angle, certain in those seconds that he is about to die.

Later, he remembers small details with disturbing clarity: the spiderweb pattern in the shattered windshield, a smear of blood on his sleeve, the helplessness of hearing voices outside the car while being unable to move. He remembers trying to lift his head and feeling a bolt of pain. He remembers the thought, simple and absolute: this is it. Even now, when he tells the story, his face goes still at that point, as if some part of him remains trapped inside the crushed frame.

His body heals faster than his mind. In the months after, friends tell him he is lucky. He nods because that seems like the correct response. He goes to follow-up appointments, does physical therapy, answers emails from clients who are relieved he is alive and eager to resume projects. Outwardly, he returns to work. Inwardly, he begins organizing his life around fear.

At first he tells himself he is just shaken. Then he notices he cannot drive on the highway without gripping the steering wheel so hard his hands ache. If a car comes too close behind him, his chest tightens and he feels a burst of heat spread through his body. He starts taking long, complicated side streets to avoid the site of the crash. When clients request meetings across town, he finds reasons to postpone, or he sends measurements and mood boards electronically rather than going in person. He had once loved visiting spaces in person, standing in a room and sensing what it needed. Now the trip there feels like something to survive.

Sleep becomes unreliable. He wakes before dawn with his heart pounding, sometimes from dreams in which he is back in the car, unable to move while impact rushes toward him again. Other times he does not remember the dream, only the terror. He keeps a lamp on in the bedroom because darkness feels too much like that trapped, airless moment. During the day he is tired, but he does not let himself rest easily. Sudden sounds—a truck downshifting, a dropped piece of metal at a job site, brakes squealing on the street—make him jerk and scan his surroundings before he can think. He hates that reflex. It makes him feel exposed, older than he is, no longer in command of himself.

His work changes in quieter ways too. He used to enjoy busy installations, multiple contractors talking over one another, the improvisation of solving problems on the spot. Now job sites leave him frayed. He startles when ladders scrape the floor. He loses track of conversations. He finds himself staring too long at exits, mentally calculating how quickly he could leave if something went wrong. Clients still see his good eye, his careful taste, but he knows how much energy it takes to appear composed. After meetings he sits alone in his car, breathing through the tremor in his hands before he can turn the key.

He is divorced, and he describes the divorce as old pain, settled into the background of his life. This is different. Since the accident, he withdraws from friends without meaning to. When they suggest dinner, he says he is busy. When they ask how he is doing, he says, “Fine, just tired.” It feels impossible to explain how a single ordinary drive has turned the world unpredictable. He is ashamed of how small his life has become. His apartment, once a place of pleasure and design, becomes more like a controlled zone. He double-checks locks, keeps pathways clear, dislikes anything out of place. Order soothes him briefly, though never for long.

What troubles him most is not only the fear but the sense that the accident keeps happening inside him. He knows, rationally, that he survived. Yet in traffic, in sleep, in the split second after a sudden noise, his body does not live in the present. It goes back to twisted metal, trapped breath, the certainty of death. He has spent a career helping other people feel at home in their surroundings. Now he moves through his own life as if danger could break through at any moment.
